skill.name: Commas that change the meaning
skill.why: One little comma can stop Grandma from becoming dinner.
skill.how: Read the sentence with and without the comma. Pick the one that means what you mean.

steps.say: A comma is tiny, but it can change everything. Read this note from my kitchen.

options.text: We're going to eat Grandma.
Grandma, come and eat with us.
options.reason: That needs a comma to keep Grandma apart. Is there one?

options.text: Grandma is doing the eating.
options.reason: Read it again: let's eat... who? Who is the food?

steps.win: Yikes! With no comma, Grandma is dinner. Let's fix that.

steps.say: I'm calling Grandma to dinner. A comma keeps her name apart from the rest.

show.nudge: Come, and eat Grandma? She is still the food! Try again.
Come and, eat Grandma? She is still the food! Try again.
A comma after Grandma? The sentence is already over there.

steps.ask: Tap the word the comma goes after, so Grandma is safe.
steps.win: Phew! Come and eat, Grandma. Now we're talking to her, not eating her.

steps.say: Talking to someone? A comma keeps their name apart. The name can come first, too.

show.nudge: This tells what Wren did. Is anyone talking to her?

show.text: Mo fed the possums with Wren.
show.nudge: Here Wren is helping. Is Mo calling her name?

steps.ask: Tap the one where Mo is talking to Wren.
steps.win: Yes! The comma after Wren shows Mo is calling her name. Then he tells her what to do.

steps.say: Tully wants the captain to phone her. She wrote this, but forgot the commas.
steps.ask: Which one shows Tully is talking to the captain?

options.text: Call me Captain when you land.
options.reason: With no commas, Tully wants to be called Captain! Keep the name apart.

options.text: Call me, Captain, when you land.
Call me, Captain when you land.
options.reason: The name is in the middle. Does it need a comma on one side, or both?

steps.win: Yes! Name in the middle? A comma on each side. Without them, Tully wants a new name!

steps.say: Commas change lists too. I made this for lunch. Count the commas carefully.
steps.ask: How many things did Mo serve?

options.text: two
options.reason: That would be jelly beans and chips. Is there a comma after jelly?

options.text: four
options.reason: Count again. Chips is the last thing, after and.

options.text: three

steps.win: Yes! The comma splits jelly from beans. Three things. Gross, but that is my cooking.

steps.say: Last one. Read it with no comma. Who sat very still?

show.nudge: While Zed... was doing what? That part isn't finished yet.
Now Zed is drawing the yeti, and 'sat very still' has no doer. Where does the while part end?

steps.ask: Tap the word the comma goes after.
steps.win: Yes! While Zed was drawing, the yeti sat very still. Read it both ways to check.

terms.means: The person you are speaking to. A comma keeps their name apart.
One thing on a list. Commas keep the items apart.

card.test: Read it with and without the comma. Which one means what you mean?

weDo.text: Mo is telling Gus that dinner is ready.
weDo.hint: Is Gus the one being spoken to, or the one being eaten?
weDo.success: The comma shows Mo is talking to Gus. Gus gets dinner instead of being dinner.

options.text: We're ready to eat, Gus.
We're ready to eat Gus.
options.reason: With no comma, Gus is the food. Poor Gus.

options.text: We're ready, to eat Gus.
options.reason: This comma is in the wrong spot. Gus is still the food.

weDo.text: We need chocolate, milk and bread.
weDo.prompt: How many things do we need?
weDo.hint: Each comma, and the word and, splits off a new thing.
weDo.success: Three. The comma splits chocolate from milk. Without it, you'd buy chocolate milk.

options.text: three
two
options.reason: That would be chocolate milk and bread. The comma splits chocolate and milk apart.

options.text: one
options.reason: The comma and the word and split the list into separate things.

creature.name: Pivvet
creature.blurb: A grasshopper from the snowy peaks that changes colour whenever a comma moves. Shift one, and the meaning hops somewhere new.

write.ask: Add a comma so Mo is talking to Gus, not about him. Then write your own line to Gus.
checks: A comma keeps Gus's name apart
My own line talks to Gus by name
Without its comma, my line would mean something else
write.model: Stop tickling, Gus. Feed the dog, Gus, before he eats my shoe.

encounters.frame: Mo is sticking a note on the igloo door for Tully.
encounters.text: Mo wants Tully to come in for dinner.
encounters.prompt: Which note should Mo write?
encounters.success: The comma shows Mo is talking to Tully. She's invited to dinner, not on the menu.

options.text: Come and eat, Tully!
Come and eat Tully!
options.reason: No comma means Tully is the dinner. She would not like that.

options.text: Come, and eat Tully!
options.reason: This comma doesn't help. Tully is still the dinner.

encounters.frame: Wren is reading her shopping receipt from the snow shop.
encounters.text: Wren bought chocolate, milk and bread for the trip.
encounters.prompt: How many things did Wren buy?
encounters.success: Three. The comma splits chocolate from milk, so they are two separate things, plus bread.

options.text: three
two
options.reason: That would be chocolate milk and bread. The comma splits chocolate and milk apart.

options.text: one
options.reason: The comma and the word and split the list into separate things.

encounters.frame: The Pivvet flashes a new colour for each sentence about Gus.
encounters.prompt: Match each sentence to what it means.
encounters.success: A comma before a name means you're talking to that person. No comma, and things happen to them.

items.text: Let's eat, Gus.
items.reason: The comma shows we're talking to Gus. He's invited to eat.

items.text: Let's eat Gus.
items.reason: No comma, so Gus is what gets eaten. Yikes.

items.text: Let's tickle Gus.
items.reason: No comma, so Gus is the one being tickled.

items.text: Stop licking, Gus.
items.reason: The comma shows Gus is being told to stop licking.

items.text: Stop licking Gus.
items.reason: No comma, so someone is licking Gus. Gross.

encounters.frame: Mo is calling Grandpa in from the snow. Don't let him get it wrong.
encounters.prompt: Tap the pieces in order so Grandpa is invited to dinner, not served as dinner.
encounters.success: The comma before Grandpa shows Mo is talking to him. Grandpa is safe.

body.reason: Put the comma just before Grandpa. That shows Mo is calling to him.

encounters.frame: Gus left three notes by the frozen slime tank.
encounters.prompt: Gus is talking to Wren. Tap the note that shows it.
encounters.success: The comma before Wren shows Gus is talking to her. Nobody is poking Wren.

parts.reason: No comma, so someone is poking Wren. Gus is talking about her, not to her.
This comma tells someone to stop. Wren is still the one being poked.

encounters.frame: Zed's spooky snow story has a scary mistake in it.
encounters.prompt: Tap the part that needs a comma, then choose the fix.
encounters.success: The yeti was just eating. The comma stops it eating the penguin, so the penguin waddles off safely.

parts.reason: This part is fine. Read on until the sentence trips you up.
This part is fine. Look at where the eating should stop.

options.text: eating, the
eating the,
options.reason: That comma splits 'the' from 'penguin'. Commas don't go between those words.

options.text: ate the
options.reason: Changing the word doesn't help. The yeti still eats the penguin. Where should the eating stop?

encounters.frame: Mission control is checking in with the rocket on the ice runway.
encounters.text: Mission control wants to ask Gus if he is ready for take-off.
encounters.prompt: Which message should they send?
encounters.success: The comma shows they are talking to Commander Gus. He's flying the rocket, not being fired off.

options.text: Are you ready to launch, Commander Gus?
Are you ready to launch Commander Gus?
options.reason: No comma means someone is launching Gus into space, like a rocket.

options.text: Are you ready, to launch Commander Gus?
options.reason: This comma doesn't help. Gus is still the thing being launched.

encounters.frame: Mo is writing up the menu from the snow festival.
encounters.text: Mo says they ate exactly three things.
encounters.prompt: Which sentence matches?
encounters.success: Chocolate cake, ice cream and jelly. The commas sit between the three things, not inside them.

options.text: We ate chocolate cake, ice cream and jelly.
We ate chocolate, cake, ice cream and jelly.
options.reason: The comma after chocolate splits it from cake. That makes four things.

options.text: We ate chocolate cake, ice, cream and jelly.
options.reason: The comma after ice splits it from cream. That makes four things.

encounters.frame: A snow possum is hungry, and a moth is in danger.
encounters.prompt: Tap the pieces in order so the moth gets away safely.
encounters.success: The comma after eating shows the possum was just eating. The moth is free to fly away.

accept: While the possum was eating, the moth flew away.
body.reason: Put the comma straight after 'eating'. Then the possum isn't eating the moth.

encounters.frame: The Pivvet is packing for the Comma Cay ice concert.
encounters.prompt: Match each sentence to how many things are on the list.
encounters.success: A comma splits two words into separate things. With no comma, they stay together as one thing.

items.text: Bring your bass guitar and drums.
items.reason: No comma between bass and guitar, so it's one bass guitar, plus drums.

items.text: Bring your bass, guitar and drums.
items.reason: The comma makes bass its own thing: bass, guitar and drums.

items.text: We need a grand piano and a stool.
items.reason: A grand piano is one thing. The stool is the second.

items.text: Bring the snare drum, a mic and a fan.
items.reason: A snare drum is one thing. Then the mic and the fan make three.

items.text: We need a piano, a stool and a fan.
items.reason: The comma and the word and split this into three things.

encounters.frame: Tully's snow footy report makes it sound like she kicked the wrong thing.
encounters.prompt: Tap the part that needs a comma, then choose the fix.
encounters.success: The comma shows Tully kicked, and then the ball rolled away. She didn't kick it into itself.

parts.reason: This part is fine. Look for where the kicking should stop.
This part is fine. Look for where the kicking should stop.

options.text: kicked, the
kicked the,
options.reason: That splits 'the' from 'ball'. Commas don't go between those words.

options.text: kicked. The
options.reason: A full stop leaves 'After Tully kicked' as a broken sentence on its own.

encounters.frame: Zed is sending messages from the ice castle level.
encounters.prompt: Zed is asking Wren a question. Tap the message that shows it.
encounters.success: The comma before Wren shows Zed is talking to her. Without it, Wren is the boss.

parts.tap: Can you beat the boss, Wren?
Can you beat the boss Wren?
parts.reason: No comma makes Wren the boss's name. Zed would be asking someone else to beat her.

parts.tap: Can you, beat the boss Wren?
parts.reason: This comma doesn't help. Wren is still the boss to beat.

encounters.frame: There's a ghost party in the frozen castle, and the vampire is nervous.
encounters.prompt: Which sentence shows the vampire got away safely?
encounters.success: The comma after eat shows the ghost was just eating. The vampire is the one who left.

options.text: Before the ghost could eat, the vampire left the party.
Before the ghost could eat the vampire, left the party.
options.reason: This comma comes after vampire, so the ghost eats the vampire. Then nobody is there to leave.

options.text: Before, the ghost could eat the vampire left the party.
options.reason: A comma after 'Before' cuts it off, and the ghost still seems to eat the vampire.

options.text: Before the ghost could eat the vampire, it left the party.
options.reason: Here the ghost eats the vampire first, then leaves. The vampire didn't get away.

encounters.frame: Everyone at the snow shelter is talking about Wren, or to her. The Pivvet is confused.
encounters.prompt: Match each sentence to what it means.
encounters.success: A comma does many jobs. Only a comma keeping the name apart shows someone is talking to Wren.

items.text: Can you help me, Wren, with the gate?
items.reason: Commas on both sides keep her name apart, so someone is asking Wren for help.

items.text: When Wren came, the wombat was stuck.
items.reason: This comma ends the when part. Wren is just someone in the story.

items.text: Did you feed the possums, Wren?
items.reason: The comma keeps her name apart at the end, so someone is asking Wren.

items.text: After lunch, Wren fed the possums.
items.reason: This comma ends the opener. The sentence tells you what Wren did.

items.text: Can you help Wren with the gate?
items.reason: No comma keeps her name apart. Someone is asked to help Wren.

encounters.frame: Gus is talking to his snow robot, Bolt. He wants Bolt to wake him up.
encounters.prompt: Tap the pieces in order so Gus asks Bolt to wake him when the snow stops.
encounters.success: The commas around Bolt show Gus is talking to the robot. Without them, Gus wants to be called Bolt.

accept: Wake me, Bolt, when the snow stops.
body.reason: Name in the middle? It needs a comma on each side. Otherwise, what is Gus asking to be called?

encounters.frame: Indi wants Mo to keep his hands off her wet mural. Her note to him says something else.
encounters.prompt: Tap the part that gives the wrong meaning, then choose the fix.
encounters.success: The note is to Mo. The comma before his name shows Indi is talking to him about the wet paint.

parts.reason: This tells you what Indi did. Is anyone being spoken to here?
This says when she painted. Is anyone being spoken to here?

options.text: don't touch, Mo
don't touch Mo!
options.reason: Shouting does not help. Who is the note talking to, and what must not be touched?

options.text: don't, touch Mo
options.reason: That comma splits two words that belong together. Who still must not be touched?

encounters.frame: The polar aquarium is painting a new sign. It should list three animals.
encounters.prompt: Which sign lists exactly three animals?
encounters.success: Sea lions, killer whales and penguins. The commas sit between the animals, never inside their names.

options.text: Come and see sea lions, killer whales and penguins.
Come and see sea, lions, killer whales and penguins.
options.reason: The comma after sea splits it off. Now you've got the sea and some lions.

options.text: Come and see sea lions, killer, whales and penguins.
options.reason: The comma after killer splits it from whales. Now 'killer' is a thing on its own.

options.text: Come and see sea lions, killer whales, penguins and seals.
options.reason: That's four animals: sea lions, killer whales, penguins and seals.

encounters.frame: Mo wrote about his hobbies. Without a comma, it sounds very strange.
encounters.prompt: Mo needs one comma so he isn't painting his nan. Tap the word it should go after.
encounters.success: A comma after painting turns it into a list: painting, his nan and his budgie. Nan stays paint-free.

parts.reason: A comma after loves splits Mo from the things he loves.
A comma after nan comes before 'and'. Nan still gets the paintbrush. Where does the first hobby end?
Nothing comes after budgie, so there's nothing to separate.

encounters.frame: Zed is writing a guidebook for the hotel on the ice moon.
encounters.text: Zed wants to say that ordinary travellers forget their snacks most of the time.
encounters.prompt: Which sentence can only mean ordinary travellers?
encounters.success: The comma after time ends the phrase 'most of the time'. Then travellers are just ordinary travellers.

options.text: Most of the time, travellers to the ice moon forget to pack snacks.
Most of the time travellers to the ice moon forget to pack snacks.
options.reason: Without a comma, 'time travellers' can stick together. Then they're people who travel through time.

options.text: Most, of the time travellers to the ice moon forget to pack snacks.
options.reason: This says most of the time travellers, as in most of a group who travel through time.

options.text: Most of the time travellers, to the ice moon, forget to pack snacks.
options.reason: These commas still leave 'time travellers' stuck together as one group.

encounters.frame: Tully is commentating the Comma Cay snow footy final. Some commas are tricky.
encounters.prompt: Match each sentence to what it means.
encounters.success: Commas round a name can mean speaking to Ash, or a bonus detail about Ash. Check who is doing what.

items.text: Kick it long, Ash, before the siren goes!
items.reason: The commas keep Ash apart, and Ash is being told to kick.

items.text: Ash, our captain, kicked it before the siren.
items.reason: These commas hug a bonus detail about Ash. Nobody is speaking to Ash.

items.text: Well played, Ash!
items.reason: The comma keeps the name apart at the end. Ash is being spoken to.

items.text: The umpire told Ash to kick it long.
items.reason: No comma keeps Ash apart. The sentence tells you what the umpire did.

items.text: When Ash kicked it, the crowd roared.
items.reason: This comma ends the when part. Ash is just someone in the story.

encounters.frame: Wren is leaving Gus a note in the messy lab.
encounters.prompt: Make the note talk to Gus. Nobody should clean Gus, or think he's the lab rat.
encounters.success: The first comma ends the when part. Commas around Gus show Wren is talking to him, not naming the rat.

accept: When you finish cleaning, Gus, feed the lab rat.
body.reason: Two commas, two jobs. One ends the when part. Where can Gus's name sit so it can't name the rat?

encounters.frame: Tully is leaving a message for the captain of the icebreaker ship.
encounters.text: Tully wants the captain to phone her when the ship arrives.
encounters.prompt: Which message says that?
encounters.success: The commas around Captain show Tully is speaking to the captain and asking for a call.

options.text: Call me, Captain, when the ship reaches the frozen harbour.
Call me Captain when the ship reaches the frozen harbour.
options.reason: No commas, so Tully wants to be called Captain. She wants a phone call instead.

options.text: Call me Captain, when the ship reaches the frozen harbour.
options.reason: Captain is still stuck to 'call me', so it's the name Tully wants to be called.

options.text: Call, me Captain, when the ship reaches the frozen harbour.
options.reason: That comma splits 'call' from 'me', so the sentence falls apart.

encounters.frame: The Comma Cay band has put up an ad. Without a comma, they'll only get two people.
encounters.text: The band needs three new members.
encounters.prompt: Tap the part that gives the wrong meaning, then choose the fix.
encounters.success: The comma splits drummer from singer, so the band gets three people: a drummer, a singer and a keyboard player.

parts: Wanted for the winter concert: a

parts.reason: Keyboard player is one person. Look for two people stuck together as one.
This part is fine. Look for two people stuck together as one.

options.text: drummer, singer
drummer-singer
options.reason: A hyphen joins them into one person who drums and sings. That's only two members.

options.text: drummer singer,
options.reason: Drummer and singer are still stuck together as one person. Where does one person end?

encounters.frame: The kitchen robot report says: Before the robot could wash, the dishwasher flooded the kitchen.
encounters.prompt: Read it without the comma. What changes?
encounters.success: With no comma, 'wash the dishwasher' sticks together. Then 'flooded the kitchen' has nobody doing it.

options.text: Nothing changes. The comma only gives the reader a short rest.
options.reason: Read it straight through with no comma. What does the robot wash now?

options.text: The kitchen floods first, and only then does the robot wash the dishes.
options.reason: The order is not the problem. What would the robot be washing?

options.text: The robot seems to wash the dishwasher, and nothing does the flooding.
The dishwasher becomes the one who wants to do the washing.
options.reason: Read it again. With no comma, what is the robot about to wash?
